# DNA replication and repair

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Genetics > Basics of genetics > DNA replication and repair*

[Original Article Link](/library/Ko0U1S)

---

## Summary

Cell division involves the duplication of a cell's entire <u>DNA</u> so that two genetically identical daughter cells arise from a single cell. <u>DNA</u> is bound to <u>proteins</u> in the <u>nucleus</u> and is tightly packed. Therefore, <u>DNA</u> replication requires that the <u>DNA</u> is loosened and the <u>double helix</u> is unwound. Specific <u>proteins</u>, including <u>DNA polymerase</u>, then synthesize a complementary <u>daughter strand</u> of double-stranded <u>DNA</u> (dsDNA) from each single strand template. This leads to the formation of two dsDNA molecules, each composed of one new and one original strand. The process of <u>DNA</u> replication includes control mechanisms to keep the genetic information as stable as possible, but errors (e.g., the incorporation of a wrong base) still occur. External factors as well as internal cellular processes lead to alterations in the chemical structure of <u>DNA</u>. Unrepaired <u>DNA</u> errors can cause mutations and/or cell destruction. <u>DNA repair mechanisms</u> are, therefore, important to ensure genomic stability.

## DNA replication

![Section 1 DNA Replication](media/small_62f0fd963dca57.31334952.jpg)

Section 1 DNA Replication




### Fundamentals of <u>DNA</u> replication




* Purpose: the process of copying dsDNA during the <u>S phase</u> of cell division, ensuring the transmission of identical genetic information from the parent cell to the daughter cell.

* <u>DNA</u> replication:

* Is semiconservative: Replication results in two identical dsDNA molecules, with each new molecule of dsDNA consisting of a parent strand (which serves as the <u>template strand</u>) and a newly synthesized daughter strand.

* Takes place in the 5′ → 3′ direction

* Is bidirectional:

* Replication occurs on both strands of the original dsDNA simultaneously in opposite directions; (i.e., the 5′→ 3′ direction of each <u>parent strand</u>).

* Two active <u>replication forks</u> are formed at the site of <u>DNA</u> double-strand separation.

* Begins at multiple points

* Occurs in three stages :

* Initiation (See “The process of <u>DNA</u> replication” in this section below.)

* Elongation

* Termination

### The process of <u>DNA</u> replication




#### Initiation



1. * Origin of replication (<u>ori</u>): a specific <u>DNA</u> sequence in the <u>genome</u> where <u>DNA</u> replication starts

* Specific <u>proteins</u> (comprising a prepriming complex) recognize and bind to the <u>origin of replication</u>.

* The <u>origin of replication</u> contains AT-rich sequences (e.g., <u>TATA box</u> regions), similar to those found in <u>promoters</u>

* <u>Prokaryotes</u> with circular genomes have a single origin.

* <u>Eukaryotes</u> have numerous <u>oris</u> (e.g., 30,000–50,000 in humans) at which <u>DNA</u> replication begins simultaneously.
2. * Replication fork: Y-shaped region in the <u>chromosome</u> where both leading and <u>lagging strands</u> are replicated from the <u>DNA</u> template

* <u>Helicase</u> separates and begins unwinding dsDNA into single strands at the <u>ori</u>, forming two <u>replication forks</u>.

* Replication occurs on both strands simultaneously (bidirectionally), but always in a 5′ → 3′ direction.
3. * Prevention of <u>reannealing</u>: SSBs prevent the single strands from <u>reannealing</u> and protect ssDNA from cleavage.
4. * <u>Supercoil</u> relaxation: : <u>DNA</u> <u>topoisomerases</u> relieve overwinding (positive <u>supercoils</u>) or underwinding (negative <u>supercoils</u>) that develop during <u>DNA</u> separation and elongation.




#### Elongation



1. * Primer synthesis

* RNA primers: a 10–12 <u>nucleotides</u> long <u>RNA</u> sequence that is complementary to the <u>template strand</u>

* Synthesized by RNA primase

* Provide a 3′-OH group to which <u>DNA polymerases</u> can attach a <u>DNA</u> <u>nucleotide</u>.

* The <u>RNA primer</u> is removed at a later stage.
2. * <u>DNA</u> synthesis: For simultaneous replication of both <u>parent strands</u>, <u>DNA</u> replication occurs continuously on the <u>leading strand</u> and discontinuously on the <u>lagging strand</u> in a 5′→3′ direction. At the same time, complementary deoxynucleotides are added to the free 3′-OH group of the <u>daughter strand</u>.  

* Reaction catalyzed by <u>DNA polymerase</u> (polymerase δ in <u>eukaryotes</u>, <u>DNA polymerase III</u> in <u>prokaryotes</u>)

* 5′→3′ DNA polymerase activity catalyzes the nucleophilic attack of the 3′-OH group on the α-<u>phosphate</u> of the incoming <u>deoxynucleotide triphosphate</u>, forming an ester bond.

* <u>DNA</u> strands are elongated by one <u>nucleotide</u> at a time.

* <u>Pyrophosphate</u> (PP<sub>i</sub>) is released.

* <u>Pyrophosphate</u> is cleaved into two <u>phosphates</u> by pyrophosphatase.

* Leading strand: a complementary <u>daughter strand</u> of <u>DNA</u> whose replication is continuous due to its free 3′-OH end

* The free 3′-OH end is initially on the primer.

* Only one primer is required.

* Lagging strand: a complementary <u>daughter strand</u> of <u>DNA</u> whose replication is discontinuous because new <u>RNA primers</u> are constantly being synthesized at the moving <u>replication fork</u> to ensure a free 3′-OH end for elongation
* Okazaki fragments; : discontinuous segments of 1,000–2,000 <u>nucleotides</u> that arise during <u>lagging strand</u> creation

* Each <u>DNA</u> segment requires its own <u>RNA primer</u>.

* Each primer is synthesized at the moving <u>replication fork</u>.
3. * Proofreading: Some polymerases (e.g., <u>DNA polymerase I</u> and III) have ; 3′→5′ exonuclease activity to proofread recently synthesized <u>DNA</u> and to remove incorrectly paired <u>nucleotides</u>.
4. * Primer removal: 

* <u>DNA polymerase I</u> and δ have 5'→3' exonuclease activity that enables the enzymes to remove the <u>RNA primer</u>.

* In <u>prokaryotes</u>; , by RNase H and 5′→3′ exonuclease activity of <u>DNA polymerase I</u>. In <u>eukaryotes</u>, the <u>RNA primer</u> is displaced by <u>DNA polymerase</u> δ and excised by the enzyme <u>FEN-1</u> (<u>flap endonuclease-1</u>)
5. * Filling the gaps: During primer removal, <u>DNA polymerase</u> fills the gaps with deoxynucleotides complementary to the <u>parent strand</u> until the free ends meet.

* In <u>prokaryotes</u>, <u>DNA polymerase I</u> replaces the <u>RNA primer</u> by adding deoxynucleotides one at a time and proofreads as it does so.

* In <u>eukaryotes</u>, polymerase δ replaces the <u>RNA primer</u>.

* <u>DNA ligase</u> joins (ligates) the free ends of <u>Okazaki fragments</u>, resulting in a continuous strand of <u>DNA</u>.

* Ligase reaction

* <u>DNA ligase</u> transfers an <u>AMP</u> residue to the 5′ <u>phosphate</u> end of one of the <u>DNA</u> fragments to be bound.

* <u>AMP</u> is cleaved and the 5′ <u>phosphate</u> end is bound to the 3′-OH end of the other fragment.




![DNA replication (leading vs. lagging strands)](media/q7sn4fvgwnmxgiqdlm9775s7.jpg)

DNA replication (leading vs. lagging strands)

![DNA synthesis mechanisms](media/w55a5fw0dmdcj9iyjhl264ej.jpg)

DNA synthesis mechanisms




#### Termination




* Initiated by binding termination <u>proteins</u> to termination sequences

* There are various termination mechanisms for circular and linear <u>DNA</u> molecules (e.g., a termination site sequence in the <u>DNA</u>).





> [!NOTE]
> <u>DNA</u> replication inhibitors have a modified 3′-OH end that prevents the elongation of the existing <u>nucleotide</u> chain, a phenomenon also known as “chain termination.”

## Telomeres

* Structure: : a noncoding <u>DNA</u> fragment of several thousand <u>base pairs</u> (composed of <u>tandem repeats</u> of TTAGGG) at the 3′ end of <u>chromosomes</u>

* Function

* Prevention of structural gene loss during replication of linear <u>DNA</u> double-strands 

* The <u>lagging strand</u>  becomes shorter with each process of <u>DNA</u> replication.

* <u>DNA polymerase</u> cannot synthesize the last part of the 5′ end of the <u>lagging strand</u> because there is no 3′-OH group present to fill the gaps following removal of the <u>RNA primer</u>.

* A section of the <u>telomere</u> is lost instead of the coding segment of the <u>DNA</u>.

* The <u>leading strand</u>  can be completely synthesized.

* <u>Telomeres</u> prevent the continuous loss of <u>nucleotides</u> from the 3′ end of <u>DNA</u> during replication and raise the number of possible replication cycles that a given cell can undergo.

* Maintenance by telomerase: a type of <u>reverse transcriptase</u> that carries its own <u>RNA</u> template (ribonucleoprotein) and can elongate <u>telomeres</u> 

* Only present in <u>eukaryotic</u> cells (especially in fast-dividing cells such as <u>stem cells</u>)

* Activity is enhanced in cancer cells

* Adds a <u>DNA</u> polymer (TTAGGG) to avoid loss of genetic material from the 3′ end of the <u>DNA</u> strand with every replication





> [!NOTE]
> To remember the TTAGGG sequence added by the telomerase: Tell Them All: Genes Gotta Go!

## Mechanisms of DNA damage

There are <u>endogenous</u> or <u>exogenous</u> sources of <u>DNA damage</u>, which may result in mutations and/or <u>cell death</u> if not repaired.




### <u>Endogenous</u> sources of <u>DNA damage</u>




* Replication errors

* Repetitive sequences: <u>DNA polymerase</u> is error-<u>prone</u> in reading repetitive <u>DNA</u> sequences. The repetitive region is repeatedly read, especially in triplet repeats.

* Keto-enol tautomerism: a transient tautomeric shift of <u>nucleotide</u> bases from the usual keto-configuration to the enol-configuration, which can result in mismatched <u>base pairing</u> (e.g., enol-<u>thymine</u> pairs with <u>guanine</u> instead of <u>adenine</u>)

* Chemical instability

* Depurination: thermal cleavage of the N-<u>glycosidic bond</u> between deoxyribose and a <u>purine</u> base  at body temperature 

* An apurinic/<u>apyrimidinic site</u> (<u>AP site</u>) is formed.

* <u>AP sites</u> belong to the most common physiologically occurring <u>DNA</u> lesions (estimate of > 10,000/day and per cell in <u>eukaryotes</u>).

* Free radical damage: highly reactive oxygen or hydroxyl radicals that cause oxidative <u>stress</u> and can chemically alter bases

* Example: <u>guanosine</u> to 8-oxoguanosine

* Result: During replication, <u>8-oxoguanosine</u> pairs with <u>adenine</u> and not <u>cytosine</u>.

* Spontaneous <u>deamination</u> of <u>DNA</u> bases causes incorrect <u>base pairing</u> (mismatching) 

* <u>Deamination</u> of <u>cytosine</u> to <u>uracil</u> (e.g., as a result of nitrite uptake in food), which then pairs with <u>adenine</u>

* <u>Uracil</u> is usually recognized as an error and replaced with <u>cytosine</u> through <u>base excision repair</u>.

* If this does not occur, <u>uracil</u> pairs with <u>adenine</u> instead of <u>cytosine</u> with <u>guanine</u> during the next replication.

* <u>Deamination</u> of 5-methylcytosine;   to <u>thymine</u>, which pairs with <u>adenine</u> instead of <u>guanine</u>.

* <u>Deamination</u> of <u>adenine</u> to <u>hypoxanthine</u>

* <u>Deamination</u> of <u>guanine</u> to <u>xanthine</u>

### <u>Exogenous</u> sources of <u>DNA</u> errors




* Toxic substances

* Alkylating substances

* Mechanism of action: methylate or ethylate bases cause incorrect <u>base pairing</u>, e.g., O<sup>6</sup>-ethylguanine is formed by the alkylation of <u>guanine</u> and pairs with <u>thymine</u> instead of <u>cytosine</u>.

* Examples: <u>mustard gas</u>, N-nitrosodimethylamine, dimethyl sulfate

* Intercalating substances

* Mechanism of action: embedding between the stacked <u>DNA</u> <u>base pairs</u>, causing replication to stop and increasing the risk of strand breaks

* Examples: ethidium bromide, acridine dye, <u>dactinomycin</u>

* Radiation

* UV radiation (both UVA and <u>UVB</u>) can result in dimer formation of neighboring <u>pyrimidine</u> bases (pyrimidine dimers) 

* Mainly formation of <u>thymine</u> dimers, linked by a cyclobutane ring

* Dimers create bulky helix distortions that interfere with <u>DNA</u> replication, which stops replication prematurely, increasing the risk for further mutations (e.g., <u>BRAF gene</u> mutation in <u>melanoma</u>).

* Ionizing radiation  

* Mainly causes dsDNA breaks, but can also cause ssDNA breaks [[1]](/library/UJbbtu)

* Also results in increased formation of <u>free radicals</u>

## DNA repair mechanisms

| Type of <u>DNA repair</u> | Phase of <u>cell cycle</u> | Mechanisms | Associations with defective repair |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ssDNA repair |  |  |  |
| Base excision repair | <br>* Throughout <u>cell cycle</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Base-specific glycosylase</u> (<u>DNA glycosylase</u>) recognizes and removes damaged bases (e.g., <u>deaminated</u> or oxidated), creating an <u>AP site</u> (apurinic/apyrimidinic).<br><br>* <u>AP endonuclease</u> cuts the <u>DNA</u> backbone on the 5′ end of the <u>AP site</u>.<br><br>* <u>AP lyase</u> cuts the <u>DNA</u> backbone on the 3′ end of the <u>AP site</u>.<br><br>* <u>DNA polymerase-β</u> refills the gap.<br><br>* Ligase reseals the strand.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Repair of spontaneous or toxic <u>deamination</u><br><br>* Certain cancers, e.g., <u>colorectal cancer</u> (MBD4), <u>gastric cancer</u> (NEIL1) [[2]](/library/A7YRoq)<br><br><br> |
| Nucleotide excision repair | <br>* <u>G1 phase</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Specific endonucleases recognize the damaged area (e.g., <u>pyrimidine dimers</u> that distort the <u>DNA</u> helix) of <u>nucleotides</u> (typically a 12–24 bp section).<br><br>* Oligonucleotide containing the damaged region is excised by <u>endonuclease</u>.<br><br>* <u>DNA polymerase</u> refills the resulting gap.<br><br>* Ligase reseals the strand.<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Xeroderma pigmentosum</u> (UV radiation causes formation of <u>pyrimidine dimers</u>)<br><br> |
| DNA mismatch repair | <br>* <u>S phase</u><br><br> | <br><br>* The newly synthesized strand (unmethylated strand) is differentiated from the <u>methylated</u> <u>parent strand</u><br><br>* Mismatched <u>base pairs</u> are recognized by <u>MSH</u> <u>proteins</u>.<br><br>* The damaged strand is cut by <u>endonuclease</u>.<br><br>* Damaged <u>nucleotides</u> are removed by exonuclease.<br><br>* <u>DNA polymerase</u> refills the resulting gap (no loss of <u>DNA</u> material).<br><br>* Ligase reseals the strand.<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer</u><br><br> |
| <br>dsDNA break repair <br> |  |  |  |
| Nonhomologous end joining | <br>* Throughout <u>cell cycle</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>DNA</u> that has undergone a double-stranded break is repaired via <u>DNA ligase</u> IV.<br><br>* Short homologous sequences called microhomologies comprise the single-stranded tails of the <u>DNA</u> ends to be joined.<br><br>* Repair is usually accurate if microhomologies are compatible<br><br>* <u>Nonhomologous end joining</u> is itself <u>prone</u> to errors and mutagenic defects because no error-free template is available.<br><br>* Some <u>DNA</u> may be lost or translocated in the process.<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Ataxia-telangiectasia</u><br><br> |
| Homologous recombination repair | <br>* Late <u>S phase</u> or <u>G2 phase</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Repair by exchanging homologous segments between two <u>DNA</u> molecules (<u>sister chromatids</u>)<br><br>* The error can be repaired using the complementary strand from the intact <u>sister chromatid</u>.<br><br>* Requires a (nearly) identical sequence (such as the complementary strand) to serve as a template for repair<br><br>* No <u>DNA</u> is lost in the process.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Breast</u>/<u>ovarian cancer</u> (due to <u>BRCA1</u> and <u>BRCA2</u> mutations)<br><br>* <u>Fanconi anemia</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Enzymes of <u>base excision repair</u>: GEL PLease = Glycosylase, AP-Endonuclease, Lyase, <u>DNA</u> Polymerase, <u>DNA</u> Ligase




> [!NOTE]
> Excision repair occurs in the <u>G1 phase</u> of <u>the cell cycle</u>. <u>DNA mismatch repair</u> occurs in the <u>S phase</u> of <u>the cell cycle</u>.
